To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

heterozygous mutations of the tumor suppressor PATCHED provoke basal-cell carcinoma-like features in normal human skin organ cultures, which is the first demonstration of a physiological impact of PATCHED mutations in keratinocytes.
heterozygous mutations of PATCHED provoke basal-like carcinoma-like features in organotypic skin models, and this is associated with an increase of GLI1 and cyclin D1.

PATCHED+/− human keratinocytes show increased proliferation, differentiation impairment, and invasiveness, as well as increased expression of GLI1 and cyclin D1, which are known to play a role in tumor formation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of human skin cancer.
the study of the molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in skin carcinogenesis and in particular in basal cell carcinoma (BCC).

the development of a novel in vitro model of human basal cell carcinoma that will allow to study the molecular mechanisms of basal cell carcinomas, to test the efficacy of new drugs and to develop new therapies for basal cell carcinoma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the PATCHED+/− mutation is not sufficient for the development of basal cell carcinoma, but that the PATCHED gene has a haploinsufficient function and that its loss is associated with a predisposition to develop basal cell carcinoma.

PATCHED+/− mutations in human skin cells lead to a basal cell carcinoma phenotype, which is characterized by hyperplasia, hyperkeratinization, increased proliferation, increased cyclin D1 expression, and impaired differentiation.
PATCHED heterozygosity leads to a basal cell carcinoma-like phenotype, and that this phenotype is associated with a deregulated SHH pathway.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
heterozygous mutations of PATCHED provoke basal carcinoma-like features in organotypic skin models.
heterozygous mutations of PATCHED gene in human organotypically cultured keratinocytes induce basal cell carcinoma-like phenotype.
the PATCHED gene is a tumor suppressor gene that acts by repressing SHH signaling in normal cells and that its loss of function in one allele is enough to induce cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PATCHED+/− human keratinocytes, when cultured in organotypic conditions, display a phenotype reminiscent of early basal cell carcinoma.
PATCHED+/− human keratinocytes are a powerful model for the study of early steps of basal cell carcinoma development.
PATCHED+/− cells are more sensitive to SHH than WT cells.
